title: Course Schedule (order)
prompt:
There are numCourses courses labelled 0 to numCourses - 1. Each pair [course, prerequisite] in prerequisites means you must take prerequisite before course.

Write findOrder(numCourses, prerequisites) that returns any order in which you can take all the courses. If it is impossible (the prerequisites form a cycle), return an empty array [].

findOrder(4, [[1, 0], [2, 0], [3, 1], [3, 2]]);
// [0, 1, 2, 3] or [0, 2, 1, 3]: both are fine

findOrder(2, [[1, 0], [0, 1]]);
// []  (0 needs 1 and 1 needs 0)

Constraints: up to 2,000 courses and 5,000 pairs. The tests accept any valid order.

tests.name: the example: any valid order of 4 courses
no prerequisites: every course appears once
tests.code:
const order = findOrder(3, []);
assertEqual([...order].sort((a, b) => a - b), [0, 1, 2]);

tests.name: a single chain must come out in exactly one order
a longer cycle hidden behind valid courses is still impossible
a course that is its own prerequisite is impossible
a bigger graph with shared prerequisites

hints: Trigger: "prerequisites", "dependencies", "must happen before", "build order". That is topological sort on a directed graph.

Idea (Kahn's algorithm): count, for each course, how many prerequisites it still needs. Courses that need 0 can be taken now: put them in a queue. Each time you take a course, every course it unlocks needs one fewer; when one drops to 0, it joins the queue. If you finish with fewer than numCourses taken, the rest are stuck in a cycle.

Code shape: unlocks = array of arrays, needs = new Array(n).fill(0); for each [course, pre]: unlocks[pre].push(course); needs[course]++. Then a queue loop that pushes onto order and decrements needs[next]. Return order.length === n ? order : [].
explain:
Time O(V + E) where V is the number of courses and E the number of prerequisite pairs: each course enters the queue once and each edge is looked at once. Space O(V + E) for the adjacency list.

Say it: "Prerequisites form a directed graph, and a valid order is a topological sort. I'll track in-degrees, start with everything that has none, and peel courses off; if some never reach zero, there's a cycle and I return empty." The same algorithm orders build steps in a monorepo, database migrations, and spreadsheet cell recalculation.
